claim_verdicts.evidence: Every frame traced after a change ran the steps in this order: UpdateLayoutTree (style recalculation: which CSS applies to which element), then Layout (when needed), then PrePaint/Paint, then raster/draw. The lesson's 'a few steps' list omits compositing/raster, which is fine at this level; the order stated is what the trace shows.

claim_verdicts.source: Chrome 153.0.8010.53 headless via CDP (Tracing devtools.timeline), reviewer scratch run on git show stage-0:www/*.html served from 127.0.0.1:8099; no HTML/MDN/Chrome docs root in versions.yaml, none under refs/
claim_verdicts.evidence: Kind is behavior, not opinion (see issue). Changes spread over many tasks: setInterval(0) changing h1 text for 1 s -> 256 DOM mutations, 62 Layout, 124 Paint: renders again and again, but not once per change. Changes in one tight synchronous loop: 1000 changes -> 1 render after the loop. The ledger text holds only for changes made across tasks; the lesson's 'in a tight loop' wording is contradicted.
claim_verdicts.suggested_text: A page that keeps changing its DOM, task after task, many times a second, makes the browser render again and again. (Changes made inside a single task are rendered together, once, after it ends.)

issues.quote: A page that changes its DOM in a tight loop, many times a second, makes the browser render again and again
issues.text: A 'tight loop' is one synchronous task; the prerequisite lesson taught that the browser cannot render during a task. Trace: 1000 DOM changes in one synchronous loop -> exactly 1 Layout and 1 Paint, after the loop. Repeated rendering needs changes spread over many tasks (timer ticks: 256 changes -> 62 renders in 1 s). As written, §4 contradicts frontend.l1.the-event-loop and invites a wrong mental model.
issues.fix: Replace with: "A page that keeps changing its DOM, task after task, many times a second (on every timer tick or mouse move), makes the browser render again and again, and the more each change moves other elements, the more work each time." Update ledger claim 8 to the suggested_text in its claim verdict.

issues.quote: the browser has no reason to render again unless the window changes or you change the page yourself
issues.text: Too strong: selecting text with the mouse and moving focus with Tab also render the page again (trace: Layout 3, Paint 7) without resizing or editing anything.
issues.fix: Use claim 5's suggested text: "...It renders again only when something from outside changes what is visible: you resize the window, select text, or edit the page in the developer tools." Update ledger claim 5 to match.

issues.text: Ledger claim 8 is a statement about browser behaviour (how often rendering runs), not an opinion; labelling it opinion with needs_verification false kept the 'tight loop' error out of verification.
issues.fix: In frontend.l1.render.meta.json claim 8: set kind to "behavior", needs_verification to true, and text to the suggested_text given for claim 8.

issues.quote: Changing the colour of a heading changes no sizes or positions, so the browser can skip layout and only paint the heading again.
issues.text: The diagram's first step is 'match CSS to elements'. For a colour change the text says layout is skipped and paint runs, but not whether the matching step runs again. I could not tell whether a CSS change always re-runs that first step.
issues.fix: Add half a sentence saying what happens to the first step, e.g. 'it re-matches the heading's styles, skips layout, and only paints the heading again'.

issues.quote: Now imagine a page that changes its DOM sixty times a second, or one that changes a single colour. Does the browser do the same amount of work for both
issues.text: The two pages differ in two ways at once (how often, and what kind of change). The lesson mostly answers 'what kind' (colour vs size), so the comparison I was primed for is only half answered.
issues.fix: Make the contrast match the answer: 'a page that changes a heading's colour, and one that changes its size', or keep 'sixty times a second' and contrast it with 'once'.
